topics: 🏷️ New Chapter: Redeeming a Field Outside the Jubilee's Fixed Rate — the owner bids first
🥚 An Issar or an Egg? — the man who underbid on his own inferior field
📉 The Falling Auction — what happens when a bidder reneges, one after another
➕ The Owner's Extra Fifth — worked examples of exactly what he must pay
⚖️ Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel — must the owner's fifth apply to the other bidder's raise too?

overview.title: 📖 Overview: Auctioning a Consecrated Field
overview.subtitle: Arakhin 27a–27b
overview.hebrewSource: הַמַּקְדִּישׁ אֶת שָׂדֵהוּ בְּשָׁעָה שֶׁאֵין הַיּוֹבֵל, אוֹמֵר לוֹ: פְּתַח אַתָּה רִאשׁוֹן
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: Having closed out the fixed-rate rules that apply to a field consecrated near the Jubilee, the daf opens a new chapter about consecrating a field at a time when no fixed 50-sela rate applies — its redemption price is simply whatever it's worth, determined by open bidding. The mishna requires the original owner to open that bidding, since he alone pays an extra fifth on top of his bid. The Gemara works through a real incident of a lowball bid, and then a detailed mishna choreographs what happens as bidders progressively drop out of a rising auction, down to the exact sela-by-sela arithmetic of the owner's mandatory fifth.

slides.title: 🏷️ New Chapter: The Owner Opens the Bidding
slides.subtitle: When there's no fixed Jubilee-rate, the field goes to auction
slides.label: The rule:
slides.text: When a field is consecrated at a time the Jubilee rate doesn't apply, the treasurer tells the owner: 'You bid first.' Why single him out? The Gemara offers three reasons: since the field is dear to him, he'll likely bid it up; the mitzva of redemption belongs first to the owner by Torah law; and — the mishna's own stated reason — only the owner pays an extra one-fifth on top of his bid, so starting with him benefits the Temple treasury most.
slides.hebrewSource: שֶׁהַבְּעָלִים נוֹתְנִין חוֹמֶשׁ, וְכׇל אָדָם אֵין נוֹתְנִין חוֹמֶשׁ

slides.title: 🥚 The Man Who Bid 'An Issar'
slides.subtitle: A real incident, and Rabbi Yosei's correction

lines.speaker: The owner
lines.text: Consecrating his own low-quality field, told to bid first: 'It is mine — for an issar!' (a tiny coin).

lines.speaker: R' Yosei
lines.text: He didn't actually say 'issar' — he said 'an egg'! Consecrated property may be redeemed with money OR with money's equivalent value, like produce.

lines.speaker: Treasurer
lines.text: 'The field has come into your possession' — the bid stands. He loses his issar (or egg) and gets the field back.

lines.speaker: Gemara
lines.text: This isn't really about whether an item's worth counts as money — everyone agrees it does. The real dispute is whether you may redeem with something whose one-fifth surcharge is worth less than a peruta: the first tanna requires at least an issar's worth; Rabbi Yosei allows even an egg.

slides.title: 📉 New Mishna: The Falling Auction
slides.subtitle: Bids of 10, 20, 30, 40, 50 sela — what happens as bidders drop out
rows: His property covers the 10-sela gap; field goes to the 40-sela bidder
Only if the 40-sela bidder still stands by his bid
His property covers the 10-sela gap; field goes to the 30-sela bidder
Same condition applies at each step
Field is sold at its real value; the 10-sela bidder's property covers any remaining shortfall
Two bidders renege at the SAME time
The gap is split between them, not charged entirely to one
Distinguishes simultaneous reneging from one-after-another reneging

slides.title: ➕ Calculating the Owner's Extra Fifth
slides.subtitle: Owner bid 20; another bidder tops him — how much does the owner ultimately pay?

steps.content: 1️⃣ Equal bids (both say 20): the owner wins automatically, since his bid effectively includes a mandatory extra fifth
2️⃣ Other bidder says 21 → owner pays 26 (his 20 + a fifth of the eventual total, plus covering the 1-sela gap)
3️⃣ Other bidder says 25 → owner pays 30 — the owner adds a fifth only to his own bid, never to the other party's raise
4️⃣ Other bidder says 26 (exceeding what the owner's fifth alone can cover) → owner may still win by paying 31 sela and a dinar, or else the treasurer tells the outbidder: 'it's yours'

slides.title: ⚖️ Why the Fifth Matters Here but Not for Second Tithe
slides.subtitle: Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel also dispute a related fine point

boxes.title: Consecrated Field (Hekdesh)
items: The extra fifth is a gain for the Temple treasury
So an owner's bid (with its guaranteed fifth) beats an equal bid from anyone else
Beit Shammai/Beit Hillel dispute (per Rav Ḥisda): if a court of three already appraised the field at another bidder's price, does the owner's fifth apply to THAT raised sum too?

boxes.title: Second Tithe (Ma'aser Sheni)
items: The extra fifth there benefits the owner himself, not the Temple
So a mishna elsewhere favors whichever bid raises the principal more, regardless of who adds a fifth
Shows the general principle: whoever's fifth profits the Temple determines whose bid 'wins' in a tie

summary.principle: When a consecrated field has no fixed Jubilee-based rate, its redemption is set by open bidding in which the original owner is required to go first and — uniquely — must add a mandatory fifth to his own bid, a rule worked out through precise auction mechanics and careful attention to whose fifth actually benefits the Temple treasury.

flowSteps.content: 🏷️ Owner opens the bidding for his own field, since only he pays an extra fifth
🥚 A too-low bid ('an issar' or even 'an egg') still binds the bidder, per the dispute over redeeming with a fraction-of-a-peruta fifth

columns.content: 📉 Reneging bidders' property covers the shortfall down the chain — split if two renege together
➕ The owner's mandatory fifth applies only to his own bid, never to another's raise

flowSteps.content: ⚖️ The Temple always benefits from whoever's fifth is larger — unlike second-tithe redemption, where the fifth benefits the owner and doesn't decide the winning bid
🎓 Key Principle: an open bidding auction can be regulated down to the last dinar to guarantee the Temple treasury never comes out behind

quiz.q: Why does the mishna require the ORIGINAL OWNER to open the bidding when a consecrated field (without a fixed Jubilee-rate) is redeemed by auction?
o: Because he is legally obligated to buy it back regardless of price
Because only the owner is required to add an extra one-fifth to his bid, which benefits the Temple treasury
Because other bidders are legally barred from bidding first
Because the owner always offers the lowest price
quiz.e: The mishna's stated reason is that the owner, unique among bidders, must add an extra fifth to his payment — starting the bidding with him is advantageous to the Temple treasury, alongside the practical reasons that the field is dear to him and that redemption is his mitzva by right.

quiz.q: In the incident of the man who bid 'an issar' for his own field, what does the ensuing Gemara discussion reveal the dispute with Rabbi Yosei is really about?
o: Whether he actually owned the field
Whether one may redeem consecrated property with an item whose one-fifth surcharge is worth less than a peruta (a tiny coin)
Whether redemption bids must be made in the Temple itself
Whether the field was properly consecrated in the first place
quiz.e: The Gemara clarifies that everyone agrees money's-equivalent value counts as money; the actual dispute is whether an item like an egg, whose one-fifth surcharge doesn't even reach a peruta's value, can still be used to redeem — the first tanna requires at least an issar's worth, Rabbi Yosei permits even less.

quiz.q: According to the mishna's falling-auction rules, if the bidder who offered fifty sela reneges and the forty-sela bidder still stands by his bid, what happens?
o: The field is sold at its assessed value with no penalty to anyone
The property of the fifty-sela bidder covers the ten-sela gap, and the field goes to the forty-sela bidder
The field is given for free to the forty-sela bidder
All prior bidders must renegotiate from scratch
quiz.e: The treasurer collects the ten-sela shortfall (fifty minus forty) from the reneging bidder's property, and the field is then redeemed by the next-highest bidder, who offered forty.

quiz.q: According to the mishna's worked example, if the owner bids 20 sela and another person bids 25 sela, how much does the owner ultimately pay to win the field?
o: 25 sela, matching the other bidder exactly
20 sela with no additional payment
30 sela — the owner adds a fifth only to his own original bid of 20, not to the other bidder's addition
26 sela, adding a fifth to the other person's bid
quiz.e: The mishna specifies that the owner adds one-fifth only to his own bid (20 + 1/4 of 20 = 25, rounded to reach the other's offer, then structured so the total comes to 30), never adding a fifth to the amount by which the other bidder exceeded him.

quiz.q: Why does the extra one-fifth surcharge determine the winning bidder in a consecrated-field auction, but NOT in a comparable second-tithe (ma'aser sheni) redemption?
o: Because second-tithe redemptions never involve extra payments
Because in the field case the extra fifth benefits the Temple treasury, while in the second-tithe case the extra fifth belongs to the owner himself, so only the principal amount matters there
Because second-tithe items cannot legally be auctioned
Because the fifth only applies to land, never to produce
quiz.e: The Gemara explains that the field's extra fifth is a genuine gain for hekdesh (the Temple treasury), making the owner's bid preferable in a tie; but for second tithe, the fifth simply returns to the same owner, so the mishna there favors whichever bid raises the actual principal, regardless of who pays a fifth.
